messages.subject_clean: Combination of point count and line transect methods
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

As part of my PhD I've carried out breeding bird surveys on blanket bog habitat. For a couple of reasons I ended up doing both line transect and point count surveys (each of our sites was surveyed with both point counts and line transects, with approximately the same effort).

I've used Distance to calculate bird abundances at each site separately for point count and transect surveys and now I'm wondering is there any way to combine the abundance estimates from the two survey types into a single density value for each species (other than just taking an average value).

Any ideas or papers related to this topic would be appreciated!

Thanks!

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] Combination of point count and line transect methods
messages.body_plain:
Hi Colin,

I think that combining densities derived from point counts and transects should be quite straightforward. I think you simply need to weight the contribution of each estimate to the combined density according to the effective area sampled. This weighting should obviously take into account sample size (number of point counts and total length of transects) but the question of how number of point counts translates (in effort terms) to length of transect depends, I think, on detectability. For a species with very low detectability (e.g. assuming unrealistically that detection probability is 100% up to10m and 0% beyond this) then 10 point counts might only effectively sample an area of 10*10*10*pi = 3142m2, which would be equivalent to the area sampled by a transect length of 157m. On the other hand, if effective detection distance was 100m, the area sampled by 10 point counts would be 10*100*100*pi, which is 314159m2, and would be equivalent to 15.7km of transects!

I think you can approximate effective detection distance from a given density by working out the total area that would contain the number of animals you encountered on your survey if they were at this density, and then working out what distance from your sampling points or lines would give you this area.

Cheers,

Mark

messages.body_plain:
Hi Colin et al.,

I think Mark's idea is heuristically appealing but what might be the right weighting is not a simple question to answer. In a way, one might argue that the weights should be, if one can assume both points and lines to be unbiased, inversely proportional to the variance associated with each estimate. But other options are certainly possible, like the effective area covered... Not sure how to define what is optimal though.

I think ideally you would set up a hierarchical model where you observe the same reality, density, with two observation modes, lines and points. Then there are parameters associated with each detection mode but they both allow inferences over a common process. I can only assume this has been done before, but off the top of my head I can't find a reference for it. Maybe some of the hierarchical models in say Andy royle or Marc Kery papers/books already do this? Dave Miller's paper suggested by Eric might be a good starting point, it does kind of that in a way, by correcting each component of the survey, lines and points, for detectability first, then modelling density over space as a function of covariates.

Cheers,

Tiago

messages.body_plain:
Hi DS community,

I have recently obtained an odd SE/cv resultS with my CT-DS data when bootstrapping and I'm wondering if you can help me figure out why this has happened?

The data are from a CT survey with 149 cameras deployed for approx. two weeks. 66 (44%) of the cameras had detections.

When running dht2, I get some sensible results:
Estimate    se       cv         LCI        UCI         df
4.6328       1.213  0.262  2.7861  7.7036   168.649

But when I run bootdht I get these results, with the high SE and CV suggesting something isn't right:
median  mean   se           lcl       ucl       cv
5.19       17.4      380.73   3.07   7.58    73.42

Does anyone know why this might be? I'm happy to provide code and data files if that's useful.

Many thanks for your help!

Verity

messages.body_plain:
Verity, you’ll have noticed that your bootstrap confidence limits are more-or-less OK.  Most (more than 97.5%) of your bootstrap estimates are probably perfectly OK, but in a small number of bootstrap resamples, you’re getting an exceptionally large estimate of population size.  You would probably need to look through the bootstrap estimates, and identify those very large ones, and look at the data from the corresponding resample to understand what is going on.  Perhaps 1 or 2 of your cameras recorded many detections very close to the camera – possibly a result of animal response to the camera, or of a well-used track passing very close to the camera.  Resamples that select such cameras more than once may cause the difficulty.  If you can identify the cause, it may suggest a solution (e.g. left-truncation if the cause is animal reaction to the camera).  Or you might just opt to stick with the analytic estimates …

Steve Buckland

Greetings Simone

There is an argument fitted.model​ in the function make.density​ in the dsims​ package. The documentation for make.density​ describes that argument as taking:

> gam object created using mgcv​ with only x and y as explanatory covariates.

That should take you to the mgcv​ package documentation to describe the use of the function  gam​ using x- and y- coordinates from your GPS animal locations as predictors.

There is lots of sophistication associated with the gam​ function, but for your purposes, I would suspect you can fit a relatively simple model to generate an object you can feed into make.density​.

Here is a crude example of gam​ at work, first generating simulated data using gamSim​

library(mgcv)
set.seed(2) ## simulate some data...
dat <- gamSim(1,n=400,dist="normal",scale=2)
b <- gam(y~s(x0)+s(x1),data=dat)
class(b)
summary(b)
plot(b,pages=1,residuals=TRUE)
vis.gam(b)

Eric is correct you can pass in an mgcv gam object and as he said it can only contain x and y as the explanatory covariates.

Hello Hridi,

To be able to apply distance sampling, you need to be able to measure or estimate distances between cameras and the animals you detected. Did you collect reference images or videos during your survey, or use automated methods to estimate distances?

Assuming you have the distances to animals, you can include covariates of detectability specific to observations of animals in your data to model the effect of species or body size on the rate at which detection probability declines with distance. This is called Multiple Covariate Distance Sampling (MCDS) which is described in the distance sampling books as well as articles, and which is implemented in the Windows Distance software and Distance R packages. If your format your data as a flatfile (one row per observation of distance, with empty rows for locations where no animals were sampled) then it shouldn't be difficult to include the covariates and import them into the software.

MCDS is briefly described by Thomas et al. 2010 which is available here: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1111/j.1365-2664.2009.01737.x

Eric H

messages.body_plain:
Good day Hridi,

We do not recommend using AIC alone for model selection with CTDS data because CTDS data collection (with t = e.g., 1 to 5 seconds) severely violates the assumption that detections are independent events. P-values of GOF tests are also invalid. See Howe et al. (2019) for an explanation and alternative approaches to model selection. https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.13082 . It's possible that the adjusted model is overfitting, and a simpler model is actually more appropriate for estimation. I see you're using the 'nadj' argument to specify the number of adjustment terms. That's good. I'll assume you also fitted an unadjusted hazard rate model. How does the fit of that model look? Is there a "shoulder" to the detection function, or does detection probability drop off sharply at short distances? The latter situation is problematic.

Density for Windows sometimes does a better job of fitting hazard rate models to CTDS data than the R optimizer. The most recent 'mrds' and 'ds' packages allows you to use the Distance for Windows optimizer from within R. See the documentation for the optimizer argument in the newest version of the Distance and mrds packages. You could try using optimizer = 'MCDS' in your call to ds.

It's important to look at the the probability density function of observed distances and not only the plot of detection probability as a function of distance when evaluating the fit of point transect models including CTDS models. It looks like detection probability is still near the maximum at 5 - 10 meters? I think this seems long relative to most studies of animals inhabiting dense forests with low visibility, where detection probability often drops off beyond 4-7 meters. Is this data from a large animal or an open habitat?

It looks like your data are left-truncated. This is appropriate if there is a relative lack of observations at short distances because animals at short distances from the camera were missed (went undetected; "false negative") because they could pass beneath the field of view of the camera (animals are small relative to camera height) or pass through the sector monitored before an image is captured (animals move quickly or trigger speed is slow). However, a lack of observations at short distances can also be caused by slight displacement away from the camera, e.g., because animals move around a large tree the camera is attached to, or because animals avoid coming too close to the camera. In that situation, it's better to not left-truncate. Hazard rate models fit to such data can compensate for the lack of detections close to the camera caused by "mild avoidance" of the camera. When there are fewer observations than expected at short distances, both approaches (left-truncating or not) can have unwanted effects on density estimates as described in the DS literature.

All the best,
Eric H

messages.body_plain:
Michelle

Thanks for your questions.

You wish to have estimates for each of your six-day sampling events. There are several issues here, some relate to data organisation and some relate to detection function modelling.
Data organisation
seems most straightforward to define your sampling events as strata, moving them up the data organisation hierarchy thus:
I don't know if you have multiple sites, your data don't indicate. If you do have multiple sites, you might split each site into a new project, so the region layer contains only "Period".
With this data setup, each period will have an effort (line length) associated with that period (rather than an amalgamation pooled across periods).
Your data snippet shows your transects are not visited during each period, that shouldn't cause problems
Detection function modelling
you don't mention how many species are of interest and whether you want species-specific (as well as period-specific, and perhaps site-specific) estimates of density. I'll set that issue aside for the moment.
using a global detection function with produced biased period-specific estimates of density if detectability differs between periods. This is because the global detection function is the wrong detection function for each period. The magnitude of the bias is a function of the differences in detectability functions between periods as shown in this paper
Rexstad, E., Buckland, S., Marshall, L., & Borchers, D. (2023). Pooling robustness in distance sampling: Avoiding bias when there is unmodelled heterogeneity. Ecology and Evolution, 13(1), e9684.  https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.9684
As the paper describes, you can alleviate the bias by including period as a covariate in the detection function modelling. However, with 14 periods, that is 14 covariate coefficients to be estimated, which might still be a struggle.
Unless transects D01A-D04A are unusual (you don't provide information about the number of transects you surveyed), you will have difficulty producing period-specific density estimates with reasonable precision. Before embarking upon a data reorganisation process, do some further tallies of number of detections by period. Ask yourself if you could still address your research question with seven density estimates each over a 12-day period.
Redefining the strata to encompass two sampling events rather than one will entail some data wrangling and re-import into Distance for Windows, so think about what is tractable before doing multiple data rearrangement.
It depends upon the data, but you may be faced with the choice between 14 estimates each with poor precision versus fewer estimates (combining adjacent sampling periods) perhaps with better precision.
I hope that gives you a sense of direction.

The goodness of fit results you describe are unusual and unexpected. With binned data, Cramer von Mises tests are not appropriate, so that's not a useful route to pursue.

Regarding NaN values coming from the chi-square test is a puzzle.  I examined our example data set (golftees) that ships with the mrds​ package, converting the exact distance to bins with the  trial​ configuration, without mishap:

data(book.tee.data)
detections <- book.tee.data$book.tee.dataframe # detection information
region <- book.tee.data$book.tee.region # region info
samples <- book.tee.data$book.tee.samples # transect info
obs <- book.tee.data$book.tee.obs # links detections to transects and regions
detections$sex <- as.factor(detections$sex)
detections$exposure <- as.factor(detections$exposure)

mybreaks <- c(0,.25,.5,.75,1,1.5,2,2.5,3,4)
tmp <- as.numeric(cut(detections$distance, breaks=mybreaks))
distb <- mybreaks
diste <- mybreaks[-1]

detections$distbegin <- distb[tmp]
detections$distend <- diste[tmp]

fi.mr.dist <- ddf(method='trial.fi <http://trial.fi>',
                  mrmodel=~glm(link='logit',formula=~distance),
                  data=detections,
                  meta.data=list(width=4, binned=TRUE,
                                 breaks=mybreaks))
ddf.gof(fi.mr.dist)

Examine the component output of the chi-square GOF test. Are there problems in the "distance" or "mark recapture" component of the GOF tests? That might narrow down the suspects.
